item.title: Molecular energies from sparse quantum prolate diagonalization on a trapped-ion quantum processor
item.description:
Worth a look new method — Combines quantum prolate diagonalization with compressed sensing, reducing the sample complexity from 𝒪(Ns) to 𝒪(log⁡Ns) sampled points of the autocorrelation function. Resolves molecular Hamiltonian energies to within 1 kcal/mol on trapped-ion hardware using circuits up to 448 two-qubit gates (1221 gates total).

Grade 0.398 · 1.9σ above the day's baseline · matched “Quantum singular value transformation and beyond: exponential improvements for…” · Davide Castaldo, Marvin Kronenberger, Marek Miller, Sélène Forget, Gemma C. Solomon, Kresten Lindorff-Larsen, Matthias Christandl, Markus Reiher

Asks

Can sparse sampling and matrix completion reduce the quantum execution overhead of quantum prolate diagonalization while retaining chemical accuracy under realistic noise?

Before

Standard quantum prolate diagonalization required 𝒪(Ns) samples (Stroschein 2026).

But

Demonstrated on a two-orbital active-space model of an arginine-tryptophan residue pair using first-order Trotterized time evolution; larger systems explored only numerically in the weakly correlated regime.

Tools

sparse quantum prolate diagonalization · compressed sensing / Hankel matrix completion · Hadamard test · Quantinuum Helios trapped-ion quantum computer

Abstract

We introduce sparse quantum prolate diagonalization (sparse QPD), which combines the original formulation of QPD [Phys. Rev. Res., 8(3), 033177, (2026)] with compressed sensing to exploit Hamiltonian spectrum sparsity for molecular systems. We show that sparse sampling reduces the sample complexity of QPD from O(N_s) to O(logN_s), where N_s is the number of sampled points of the autocorrelation function (i.e. distinct circuits), without increasing circuit depth at chemical accuracy. With a two-orbital active-space-embedded Hamiltonian for an interacting arginine--tryptophan residue pair in water as an example, we show that on the Quantinuum Helios trapped-ion quantum computer, sparse QPD resolves the Hamiltonian energies to chemical accuracy with circuits of up to 448 two-qubit gates. For a suitably large quantum processor, we demonstrate numerically in the weakly correlated regime that the method extends to larger systems.

item.title: Circuit compilation in the quspect quantum SDK: selecting routings after coupling-constrained resynthesis
item.description:
Worth a look new method — quspect compiler uses 0.616 times as many two-qubit gates as Qiskit O3 (95% bootstrap interval 0.555–0.679) at 0.592 times the depth across 55 arXiv circuits on five topologies.

Grade 0.389 · 1.8σ above the day's baseline · matched “Toward the first quantum simulation with quantum speedup” · Xusheng Xu, Runqing Zhang, Hongtao Xue, Jize Han, Jingwei Wen, Ruoyu Zhou, Lei Jin, Xiaoxiao Hu, Gui-Lu Long

Figure

Geometric-mean ratios of two-qubit gate count and circuit depth relative to Qiskit O3 for 275 cases (55 circuits across five coupling topologies). Values below 1.0 indicate smaller gate counts or shallower depth than Qiskit O3.

Asks

How can circuit compilation combine layout routing and synthesis to prevent routed SWAP gates from inflating post-synthesis gate count and depth?

Before

BQSKit level 2 reached 0.853 and tket 0.930 relative to Qiskit O3 two-qubit gate counts.

But

arXiv set aggregate results informed development; loses to Qiskit on random Clifford circuits on 127- and 156-qubit devices; outputs verified numerically to 10−9 tolerance per matrix element.

Tools

coupling-constrained resynthesis · parity-state A* search · merge-aware routing large-neighborhood search · numerical three-qubit block instantiation

Code. https://github.com/QuSpect/quspect

Abstract

quspect is an open-source quantum computing SDK that provides circuit construction, C++ state-vector simulation with adjoint gradients, support for variational and combinatorial-optimization algorithms, Hamiltonian simulation, control-pulse envelopes and backends for several cloud quantum processors. Here we describe and evaluate its circuit compiler. Routing and synthesis interact: inserting a SWAP can change the circuit structure that later optimization exploits. At its highest optimization level, the compiler evaluates a screened set of routing candidates by their cost after coupling-constrained resynthesis. The pipeline combines parity-state A* search for small CNOT-phase regions, heuristic synthesis for larger regions, and numerical three-qubit instantiation with a per-block 10^-9 check. For a fixed phase polynomial, A* certifies the minimum CX count when it reaches a goal within budget. On an evaluation set of 55 circuits from 41 arXiv papers on five topologies, the compiler uses 0.616 times as many two-qubit gates as Qiskit O3 (95% circuit-cluster bootstrap interval 0.555-0.679) at 0.592 times its depth. BQSKit level 2 reaches 0.853 and tket 0.930. On a 17-qubit superconducting processor, the compiled circuits had the fewest CZ gates in all six scenarios of the main run. Ablations assess the contributions within the integrated pipeline.

item.title: Exact classical bounds of bipartite correlation Bell inequalities using improved branch-and-bound
item.description:
Worth a look new method — Branch-and-bound solver with see-saw heuristic initialization and greedy row reordering computes exact classical bounds for bipartite Bell matrices up to 130×130 and 81×321, improving lower bounds to KG(3)≥1.438746, KG(4)≥1.486092, KG(5)≥1.498904, and KG(7)≥1.499667.

Grade 0.374 · 1.6σ above the day's baseline · matched “quantum algorithms with provable speedup, query and gate complexity bounds” · István Márton, Erika Bene, Péter Diviánszky, Tamás Vértesi

Figure

Best mean runtime in seconds versus matrix size n on random square matrices, comparing standard branch-and-bound (BB) to the improved algorithm (IBB).

Asks

How can exact classical bounds of two-outcome bipartite full-correlation Bell inequalities with large numbers of settings be computed efficiently?

Before

For d=3, best published rigorous lower bound on KG(3) was 1.43670 (Designolle et al. 2026). On 60×60 random matrices, standard branch-and-bound ran in mean 12854 s.

But

Worst-case search complexity remains exponential. Computational performance degrades if matrix-dependent preprocessing depth is suboptimal; cannot yet solve the 120×120 E8 matrix instance.

Tools

branch-and-bound search · see-saw iteration initialization · greedy row reordering · OpenMP shared-memory parallelization

Code. https://github.com/istvanmarton/IBB

Abstract

We present an improved branch-and-bound (IBB) algorithm for the exact computation of classical (local) bounds of bipartite correlation Bell inequalities. We strengthen pruning in the standard BB algorithm in two ways: a heuristic search based on see-saw iteration supplies a strong initial lower bound, and greedy row reordering of the Bell matrix reduces the tail bounds used during the exact search. An OpenMP implementation combines these improvements with shared-memory parallelism and dynamic work redistribution. Random-matrix benchmarks show substantial runtime reductions in matrix sizes, while explicit constructions demonstrate exact local-bound computations for square matrices up to 130 ×130 and rectangular matrices of sizes up to 81 ×321. Applications provide improved lower bounds on finite-order Grothendieck constants for d=3,4,5,7 and uniform-input XOR games with quantum-to-classical ratios exceeding √2. The method retains an exponential worst-case search for this NP-hard optimization problem, and its practical performance depends on matrix structure and tail-bound preprocessing depth.

item.title: Entanglement Lower Bounds for Symmetric Quantum Circuits
item.description:
Worth a look theory — No polynomial-size symmetric quantum circuit family with 1- and 2-qubit gates can compute 𝒫CFIAlt if its entanglement width is o(n/log⁡n). The bound holds even for symmetry restricted to Altn.

Grade 0.374 · 1.6σ above the day's baseline · matched “quantum algorithms with provable speedup, query and gate complexity bounds” · Davi Castro-Silva, Ryan Dancy, Sergii Strelchuk

Asks

Can symmetry restrictions on quantum circuits be used to establish unconditional circuit lower bounds?

But

Circuits restricted to 1- and 2-qubit gates, symmetric under input permutations (or alternating group Altn), with entanglement width at most o(n/log⁡n).

Tools

quantum pebble game · partial trace indistinguishability · Cai-Fürer-Immerman construction · entanglement width

Abstract

Symmetric circuits require every symmetry of the input to extend to an automorphism of the circuit. In the classical setting, their connection to descriptive complexity yields strong unconditional lower bounds. We extend this approach to the quantum model of symmetric computation defined by Castro-Silva, Gur, and Strelchuk (ITCS 2026), proving a tradeoff between circuit size and entanglement width (the smallest b such that, on every computational-basis input, the state after each layer factors into states on at most b qubits each). Our main result identifies a graph property decidable in classical polynomial time that no polynomial-size family of symmetric quantum circuits on n-vertex graphs with entanglement width o(n/logn) can compute. The bound holds for circuits with arbitrary one-qubit and two-qubit gates and unrestricted depth, and remains valid under the weaker notion of symmetry with respect to even permutations of vertices. Our proof is based on a new quantum pebble game based on the partial trace. The resulting indistinguishability theorem transfers classical pebble-game lower bounds to quantum circuits with restricted entanglement. By contrast, without entanglement restrictions, we show that every graph property in BQP can be computed by a uniform family of polynomial-size symmetric quantum circuits. Restricting to circuits with no entanglement at all, we show that polynomial-size symmetric quantum circuits with entanglement width 1 can compute every graph property definable in fixed-point logic with counting. Finally, we give an efficient symmetric implementation of QAOA for MAX 3XOR, providing a starting point for studying entanglement lower bounds in quantum optimization algorithms.

item.title: QEDist: Practical Exact Distance Certification for Stabilizer Codes
item.description:
Worth a look new method — Certifies exact code distances up to d=34 for stabilizer codes up to n=5278 physical qubits, verifying 88 of 95 surveyed lifted-product codes previously known only by distance upper bounds, within seconds per code on one Apple M3 Pro core.

Grade 0.373 · 1.6σ above the day's baseline · matched “Toward the first quantum simulation with quantum speedup” · Jong Yeon Lee

Figure

Search time scaled to an Apple M3 Pro reference core against exclusion cutoff weight W (left) and fraction of overlapping parity-check pairs (right) across multiple quantum LDPC code families.

Asks

Can minimum distances of large quantum low-density parity-check stabilizer codes be practically certified by exact branch-and-bound tree searches rather than bounded by heuristic witnesses?

Before

Randomized searches and linked-cluster tree searches (Dumer, Kovalev, Pryadko) provided upper bounds or scaled poorly for d≳16; exact values for many lifted-product codes remained uncertified.

But

CSS codes and non-CSS qubit stabilizer codes with sparse parity-check matrices; searches become prohibitive when check-pair overlap is low or distance exceeds accessible branch-depth budgets.

Tools

weighted-check lower bounds · stabilizer-equivalence pruning · verified permutation symmetry reduction · depth-first branch-and-bound search

Abstract

We present QEDist, a method and software package that certifies the distance of qubit stabilizer codes. Building on tree-search methods, QEDist constructs candidate logical operators one qubit at a time, using sparse parity checks, stabilizer equivalence, and verified symmetries to reduce the work. For a cutoff W, a completed search either finds a nontrivial logical operator of weight at most W or proves that none exists. Because satisfying one check can violate another, we use both satisfied and unsatisfied checks to lower-bound the weight needed to complete a logical operator, and prune branches whose bound exceeds the remaining budget, which substantially reduces net search time. We benchmark QEDist mainly on Calderbank-Shor-Steane (CSS) codes; the same formulation extends to non-CSS codes and to the fault distance of syndrome-extraction circuits. For lifted-product (LP) codes, we further exploit the product structure to replace part of the full-code search with a smaller search on a classical constituent. We establish exact distances for codes with up to several thousand qubits, including Abelian and non-Abelian LP codes whose distances were previously reported only as upper bounds. In several seconds of search on one laptop core, QEDist certifies exact distances up to 20 for many of these codes and fault distance 10 for the syndrome-extraction circuit of the [[144,12,12]] code. With orders-of-magnitude speedups over the tested exact solvers, QEDist makes exact distance certification a practical tool for selecting and optimizing finite-length quantum codes.

item.title: Proven optimality for LABS with quantum-classical branch and bound
item.description:
Worth a look new method — Proves optimality for Low Autocorrelation Binary Sequences (LABS) of lengths n=2 to 30 using a quantum-classical hybrid branch and bound (QCBB) with fixed-angle QAOA (p=12 and p=1, 1,000 shots per node).

Grade 0.365 · 1.5σ above the day's baseline · matched “Quantum Algorithm for Linear Systems of Equations” · András Czégel

Figure

Upper bound (incumbent energy, blue line) and certified lower bound (vermilion line) plotted against wall-clock time, showing convergence to the certified optimum for n=2 through 30 under QAOA and classical samplers.

Asks

Can a quantum optimization algorithm deliver a certified proof of optimality for the LABS problem rather than merely finding good heuristic solutions?

Before

Classical branch and bound proved optima up to n=66 (Packebusch and Mertens 2016), while Gurobi reached n=41; prior quantum methods only returned heuristics without bounding gap or certifying optimality.

But

Proven range limited to n≤30 in noiseless simulation; runtime node count grows by a factor of roughly 1.9 per unit n (95% interval 1.59–2.37); claims no quantum speedup.

Tools

quantum-classical hybrid branch and bound (QCBB) · fixed-angle QAOA · native quartic Hamiltonian · integer bounding with lag budgets · primal-dual integral

Abstract

Low autocorrelation binary sequences (LABS) are the phase codes of pulse compression radar and the synchronization words of digital communication, and finding the sequence of a given length whose aperiodic autocorrelations have the smallest sum of squares is a hard binary optimization problem. The quantum optimization methods tested on LABS so far return good sequences, but they cannot show that a sequence is optimal or bound how far from optimal it may be. We show that a quantum optimization algorithm can deliver proven optimality. In our quantum-classical branch and bound, fixed-angle QAOA samples the Hamiltonians of the nodes of the search tree, its samples supply candidate sequences and the branching choice, and classical bounds prune the tree, so that the algorithm returns either a proof of optimality or, if it is stopped early, the best sequence found with a certified lower bound and gap. It works on the native quartic Hamiltonian without penalty terms, and its correctness does not depend on the sampler. With QAOA at depth p= 12 and at p= 1 and 1,000 shots per node, it proved the optima of all lengths from 2 to 30, where from length 27 on the root node is split without being sampled. Every run records both bounds against time, and its primal-dual integral measures its convergence. We claim no speedup.

item.arxave:figurecaption: Upper bound (incumbent energy, blue line) and certified lower bound (vermilion line) plotted against wall-clock time, showing convergence to the certified optimum for n=2 through 30 under QAOA and classical samplers.

item.arxave:tools: quantum-classical hybrid branch and bound (QCBB) · fixed-angle QAOA · native quartic Hamiltonian · integer bounding with lag budgets · primal-dual integral
item.arxave:abstract: Low autocorrelation binary sequences (LABS) are the phase codes of pulse compression radar and the synchronization words of digital communication, and finding the sequence of a given length whose aperiodic autocorrelations have the smallest sum of squares is a hard binary optimization problem. The quantum optimization methods tested on LABS so far return good sequences, but they cannot show that a sequence is optimal or bound how far from optimal it may be. We show that a quantum optimization algorithm can deliver proven optimality. In our quantum-classical branch and bound, fixed-angle QAOA samples the Hamiltonians of the nodes of the search tree, its samples supply candidate sequences and the branching choice, and classical bounds prune the tree, so that the algorithm returns either a proof of optimality or, if it is stopped early, the best sequence found with a certified lower bound and gap. It works on the native quartic Hamiltonian without penalty terms, and its correctness does not depend on the sampler. With QAOA at depth p= 12 and at p= 1 and 1,000 shots per node, it proved the optima of all lengths from 2 to 30, where from length 27 on the root node is split without being sampled. Every run records both bounds against time, and its primal-dual integral measures its convergence. We claim no speedup.
